title: The Valladolid Debate on the Indians
text:
By 1550 Spanish conquest in the Americas had brought enslavement, forced labor and mass death to Indigenous peoples. Bartolome de las Casas, a former settler and slaveholder who had become a Dominican friar, had spent decades denouncing these abuses. His protests helped persuade Emperor Charles V to take a remarkable step: he suspended new conquests and convened a panel of theologians and jurists at Valladolid, in Spain, to decide whether the wars were just.

The case for conquest was made by Juan Gines de Sepulveda, a respected scholar who drew on Aristotle. He argued that the Indians were by nature inferior, natural slaves, and that war to subject them and Christianize them was justified.

Las Casas answered for days, reading from a long Latin treatise. He argued that the peoples of the Americas were fully rational human beings with their own societies, laws and arts, that they could only be won to Christianity by peaceful persuasion, and that the conquest was robbery and murder. The sessions continued in 1551.

The judges never issued a clear verdict, and conquest resumed. But the debate became a landmark: an empire had formally asked whether its own conquests were just.
lesson: Stand up for the humanity of others, even when your own side profits from denying it. Moral arguments can change history slowly even when they lose the day.
people: Bartolome de las Casas, Juan Gines de Sepulveda, Charles V
source: Bartolome de las Casas, Apologia (In Defense of the Indians); Domingo de Soto, summary of the disputation (1552)
